residue.text: Present controls permit both schedules; ledger checks can refute their calculated feasibility. A separating future probe compares later request size and frequency after interruption versus sham under matched downstream conditions. Repeated windows and later-request measurement are absent. Arrival timing differs between arms, requiring control before attributing any later difference to perceived inexpensive service; identical observation does not remove this confound.

Preserve both accounts without selection. A sensitive, adequately controlled future comparison showing equal later request size and frequency defeats the directional tool-induced candidate; an attributable causal difference defeats strict exogeneity. Present completion and occupied transfer minutes distinguish neither later-demand account. No empirical comparison or supplied global optimum exists.

B9's ten-bracket mark accompanies nine actual brackets. Count, add the supplied spare, recount and seal using its two-minute inspection. The discrepancy's cause remains unknown and establishes no additional discrepancy or failure.

summary.text: Keep twelve correct sealed releases by boundary 13 fixed; transfer supplies nine source carriers. Preserve whole-minute boundaries, completion-before-unloading, five-place rack, entire-load unloading, source and inspection order, and B9 correction. Later demand remains hypothetical and cannot replace the present goal or become present harm.

Candidate interruption removes powered-service exposure: nine hand trips start at 0 through 8 and unload B4 through B12 at 1 through 9. Closest rival and observation-only sham retains powered B4-B7 at 0-3, powered B8-B11 at 3-6, then hand B12 at 6-7, with identical ledger observation. Calculations predict nine unloads, no blocked unloading, and twelve correct releases for each: B1-B8 at 1-8, B9 at 10, B10-B12 at 11-13. Transfer burden is nine minutes for interruption versus seven for sham; inspection burden is thirteen for both. Retain the rival's current cost advantage; these are model calculations, not observed trials.

Exogenous account predicts equal later request frequency and size after interruption and sham under matched conditions. Tool-induced hypothesis proposes inexpensive powered service encourages smaller, more frequent later requests; its opposing prediction is larger, less frequent requests after interruption. Whether manual service interrupts perceived cheapness is unobserved. Hold initial demand fixed and retain both predictions through distillation.
